what_its_for: Ceritinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread to other parts of the body. It works in patients whose cancer has a specific change (mutation) in a gene called ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase). Your doctor will test your cancer to make sure ceritinib is right for you.
how_to_take: Take ceritinib by mouth WITH FOOD (a meal or snack) every day at about the same time. Swallow the capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or open them. Taking it with food helps reduce stomach upset and helps your body absorb the medicine better. If you vomit after taking your dose, do NOT take another dose that day — just take your next scheduled dose.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 450 mg (three 150 mg capsules) taken by mouth once daily with food. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have side effects. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS your next scheduled dose is less than 12 hours away. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ceritinib capsules at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed. Store away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine safely out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medicine through a medicine take-back program — do not flush down the toilet or throw in household trash unless the label says it is safe to do so.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating grapefruit, drinking grapefruit juice, or eating Seville oranges while taking ceritinib — these can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid taking antacids, proton pump inhibitors (like omeprazole), or H2 blockers (like famotidine) at the same time as ceritinib without talking to your doctor first. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because many medicines can interact with ceritinib. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as ceritinib may make your skin more sensitive. Women who are pregnant or planning to become pregnant should not use this medicine — it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have any of these serious warning signs: severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that does not get better; new or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or trouble breathing (possible lung problem); fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat or dizziness (possible heart rhythm problem); yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes, dark urine, or severe tiredness (possible liver problem); sudden blurry vision or other vision changes; unusual weight gain or swelling; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or fruity breath; severe skin rash or blistering. Also call your doctor if you feel generally unwell, have unusual bruising or bleeding, or if any side effect bothers you or does not go away.
when_it_works: Ceritinib does not cure cancer, but it can help slow or stop the growth of cancer cells. Some patients notice improvements in their symptoms within the first few weeks, but it may take several weeks to months before imaging scans show that the medicine is working. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you feel well, and do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Ceritinib can harm an unborn baby. Do not use if pregnant. Women of childbearing age must use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 6 months after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking ceritinib and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Liver problems: Your doctor may need to lower your dose or monitor you more closely if you have liver disease, since ceritinib is processed by the liver. Kidney problems: No dose adjustment is usually needed for mild to moderate kidney disease, but tell your doctor about any kidney problems you have. Children: Ceritinib is not currently approved for use in children. Older adults (65 and older): Older patients can take ceritinib, but may be more sensitive to side effects — report any new symptoms to your doctor promptly.
